To achieve this, we employed the CHAMP algorithm to organize the graph into a hierarchical format and the GRU-Encode algorithm to create a compact representation for each node by analyzing its local connectivity across the different layers of the graph. Our evaluation using the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach by measuring the precision at k values for k=1 to 10, and outperforming state-of-the-art methods including the Wikipedia2vec algorithm.

The concept of ideal incompatible kidney transplants has been advocated for several years, yet it has not been widely adopted in the transplantation community. We define an ideal incompatible kidney transplant as one that is performed on a deceased donor kidney with moderate end-stage renal disease symptoms, transplanted into an recipient whose blood type is not compatible with the kidney's blood type but who has already received a functioning kidney from a living related donor. Based on a analysis of 2004-2014 Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative data, we found that these ideal transplants may offer a significant survival advantage over standard deceased donor transplants for this specific population of renal disease patients. Our analysis also suggests that ideal transplants may provide a substantial renal function benefit over both deceased and living donor transplants. The research also highlights the potential for increasing the pool of deceased donor transplants by allowing crossmatches to be performed after organ retrieval.

This paper presents an overview of the implicit kernel approach, a method that
avoids explicitly forming the kernel matrix in certain problems. By utilizing
implicit factorizations of a positive definite matrix, this method reduces memory
requirements and enhances computational efficiency. An in-depth examination of
various techniques falling under the implicit kernel category is provided, along
with references to relevant methodologies. Additionally, future research
directions are discussed for communities focused on specific applications rather
than the implicit factorization methods themselves.

This paper challenges the assertion that distributed representations truly grasp the nature of stock news sentiment. We scrutinize a prevalent sentiment dataset, identify inconsistencies in its annotations and limitations in representing semantic information. Our analysis reveals that both supervised and unsupervised tasks require pretrained models to significantly surpass baseline performance using representations of either the news corpus or word-by-word. Moreover, our findings suggest that both linear and non-linear dimensions captured by both sentiment and standard representations originate primarily from surface-level characteristics rather than true semantic comprehension. Notably, surface-level features play a crucial role in enabling successful word learning during BOW learning. These insights call into question the reliance on preannotated sentiment datasets and suggest that distributed representations, much like word2vec, are influenced by stock-specific surface characteristics, primarily stemming from frequent company names. Our proposed approach involves employing a sentiment-informed LDA model to enhance classification performance by at least 10%. Finally, our experiments demonstrate that both pre-trained and custom-trained models are highly susceptible to noise in sentiment analysis. To address this issue, we recommend the use of a new, robust dataset that has been meticulously cleaned and thoroughly tested.

This paper is following the trail of our previous study that explored a range of methods to enhance both data transmission and power delivery across multiple antennas and frequency modulation, building upon single antenna systems.
Three distinct scenarios were examined in our prior research: multiple transmitters sending signals to a single receiver using multiple carrier systems, two transmitters sending data to one receiver through multiple antenna and frequency modulation, and a pair of relay systems that receive multiple transmitters and pass on their signals to a single receiver using multiple antennas and multiple carrier systems.
To bridge the gap between single antenna and two transmitters scenarios, this study delves into the performance of precoding in system-wide designs and a single relay system in this regard.
In order to compare and contrast multiple approaches, we conducted both computer simulations and real-world experiments, which included an experiment with one relay system and another with a single relay.
To achieve optimal balance between multiple antennas and frequency modulation, a range of methods was proposed, which included creating equivalent systems for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM.
These systems included a matched filter relay, an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing relay with a maximum ratio transmitter and receiver, and a direct-FM relay system.
Like in our previous studies, the relay systems utilized a range of methods to allocate both spectrum and relay resources to maximize the sum rate, which was then compared to the system-wide design in two relay systems studied previously.

A novel approach combining level-set and embedded boundary methods has been developed to address complex phenomena during the solidification and melting processes, particularly those involving significant changes in material properties and multiple phases. By utilizing a level-set function to track the interface and an embedded boundary technique to model the solid phase, we derive a discrete formulation for a 1D Stefan problem with an oscillating interface, allowing for isolated observation of specific behaviors. The proposed method's accuracy has been validated through numerical experiments under varying conditions, including periodic interface movements and random domain perturbations. Furthermore, the approach has been applied to 2D problems featuring time-dependent interface dynamics and melting patterns arising from thermal convection.

In the realm of categorial grammar, analyzing linguistic structures can be challenging due to the ambiguity that arises from unary connectives, a phenomenon absent in type-theoretic semantics where formulas and their interpretations maintain a one-to-one correspondence. Our proposed solution introduces quantum units of type $A$ as an innovative approach, drawing from the realm of linear logic. The interpretation of these units relies on the "twisted product" within the compact closed category of linearly typed lambda calculus. This solution offers benefits beyond resolving structural ambiguity, as it enables the integration of proof terms with semantic content, a feature particularly advantageous in natural language processing applications. Our demonstration utilizes the Lexical-Conceptual-Interface approach to interpret the anomaly in pronoun resolution associated with the anomaly in Donkey Primitives, ultimately presenting a fresh perspective on the interplay between syntax, semantics, and proof theory within language processing frameworks.

In multiplayer competitive situations, a rationalizable equilibrium stands as the broadest possible foundation for anticipated player behavior. Nevertheless, achieving this equilibrium through player interactions in practical applications often proves challenging due to the necessity of extensive player engagements. Our research introduces a novel approach to secure a rationalizable equilibrium through the assessment of player preferences expressed in numerical ratings. This approach necessitates solely two assessments of these expressed preferences. A theoretical analysis reveals that our approach guarantees a rationalizable equilibrium among players in games comprising three or more participants, while practical implications are demonstrated through tests among human subjects in games played for money, showing our method's ability to predict player behavior accurately and outperforming existing strategies.

This study examines two models of epidemics on networks that have undergone a process of preventive restructuring, specifically coil-partitioning, by analyzing component sizes and infected node counts. Coil-partitioning consists of interdependent modules where internal connections are stronger than external connections between modules. We derived analytical expressions for distribution functions of component sizes in a statistical mechanics framework, and these predictions are verified through Monte Carlo simulations. The results also reveal the emergence of two types of first-order phase transitions in the systems. Moreover, the investigation re-evaluates the complexities of a transition known as the cascade in the context of preventive restructuring, finding that it decomposes into two distinct transitions of different natures. Furthermore, the systems exhibiting coil-partitioning exhibit reduced vulnerability to infection spread, and the sizes of large components increase by up to an order of magnitude compared to randomly connected networks (ER).

In this study, we examine a type of geometric structure known as nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds and identify how certain properties, like being conformal Ricci or Ricci soliton, interact with this structure. We also analyze the manifold in relation to other solitons, such as gradient Ricci, and prove that the manifold is not compatible with these solitons under specific conditions. Furthermore, we introduce and explore the concept of Cotton solitons within the context of the geometric structure.

This paper outlines a framework for constructing and assessing statistical models of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) using experimental data from experiments involving high-energy hadronic interactions. The framework outlines the necessary components for such a model, including fundamental measured quantities, derived but unmeasured quantities, theoretical parameters, and experimentally determined functions based on previous measurements. The document also examines the process of fitting these models to a wide range of experimental data, considering various aspects such as correlations between data points, differing normalizations and experimental systematics across different datasets, and the choice of statistical method for fitting, particularly in light of issues related to over-constrained data fitting. A historical overview of methods for QCD PDF fitting is provided in the paper.

Deep reinforcement learning has achieved significant success due to its ability to handle complex state spaces, but its training stability remains a major challenge. To mitigate this challenge, the experience replay technique was introduced, which stores past experiences and randomly selects them for training. Although the traditional approach of uniformly sampling the experience pool has been effective, the associated computational cost of weighting the sample-based probability has been deemed excessive. To address this issue, we propose an improved technique, called variance decrease based experience replay, which focuses on selecting samples with decreasing variance. This technique aims to provide high variance samples for policy exploration and gradually provides low variance samples for policy improvement. By incorporating variance decrease based experience replay, we show that our proposed policy promotion framework can effectively promote the policy performance without incurring excessive computation cost. Our framework is evaluated on multiple state-of-the-art algorithms across various benchmarks, and the results indicate that our variance decrease based experience replay can consistently outperform the traditional approach of uniformly sampling the experience pool.

I present PyCommute, a Python library that facilitates operations on commuting operators and automatically optimizes the computation sequence to minimize expansion, reducing both memory usage and processing time. PyCommute can be utilized to design advanced features in higher-level applications by enabling precise and optimized computation of complex mathematical objects, such as the partition functions in statistical mechanics models, and can even serve as a primitive for integer arithmetic.

Recent research into multilayered cuprate superconductors has revealed the presence of authentic electronic configurations and isolated superconducting regions that exceed a certain critical depth. These regions exhibit characteristics of a d-wave superconductor. Similarities between (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ and multilayered cuprate superconductors, such as their structural and phase transition similarities, have motivated us to investigate the former using X-ray scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Our high-resolution experiments have shown that the density functional theory-predicted configuration of the superconductor matches our findings, while weak superconducting regions above the critical layer display characteristics of a s-wave superconductor.

Two methods for addressing the supersymmetric chiral random matrix ensembles have been examined, specifically the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization technique. A connection between these two approaches has been established, and subsequently, this link is demonstrated to be equivalent through a change of variables, and also through the use of path integrals. Additionally, the successful application of the superbosonization technique to calculate the microscopic orthogonal ensemble is reported.

The study of top quark polarization offers new possibilities for enhancing and validating substructure techniques, as well as searching for new physics beyond the Standard Model. In a specific analysis, a top quark's longitudinal polarization is examined through the eye-bit asymmetry in a process involving a single top quark produced via the t-channel interaction. A simulated sample of such events is used to estimate the polarization in various kinematic scenarios. Furthermore, the analysis focuses on the impact of electroweak radiative corrections, initial-state proton effects, and experimental detector influences. The findings suggest that particle-level simulations can accurately predict polarization outcomes, while the estimated polarization may be underestimated due to experimental conditions. Additionally, specific simulated scenarios are presented that could be utilized to experimentally measure top quark polarization in the t-channel process.

The critical thickness threshold of the metallic layer found at the boundary of LaAlO$_3$ and SrTiO$_3$ has been the subject of extensive research for a significant period. In contrast, the metallic layer within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ structures exhibits n-type doping and remains nonferromagnetic, in stark contrast to its bulk counterpart's ferromagnetic properties. By utilizing $\beta$-detected NMR, we measured the spin-lattice relaxation rate in ultrathin LaNiO$_3$ layers (thickness ranging from one to three units cell) as a function of temperature. Our findings reveal a marked reduction in the spin-lattice relaxation rate in these ultrathin LaNiO$_3$ layers in comparison to both their bulk form and medium-thickness form. This reduction is most prominent at the Néel temperature, offering new insights into the electronic and magnetic properties of these materials.

In our effort to investigate the challenges of conversational multi-turn navigation, we are presenting a complex dataset called MultiTalk, characterized by highly branching dialogue trees that vary widely in the topics discussed. Unlike previous works, we explored the challenges of navigation in highly branching dialogue structures, rather than linear stories. To accomplish this, we initially hand-crafted a simple, 3-way branching dialogue test set consisting of everyday situations, including issues with home appliances. To evaluate the limitations of existing NavBot models in this context, we created two new metrics to assess performance at junction points in the dialogue trees. Our experimental results led to the development of several NavBot strategies, ultimately prompting the creation of an intricate, topic-aware navigation model utilizing large language models and topic similarity scoring, achieving a surprising 90% success rate in our test set.

This paper offers an analytical study on the likelihood of reliable communication in two types of wireless transmission models: one involving a large number of unconnected devices and another involving a single connected device. We examine how correlation and phase shift patterns affect these models by analyzing large-scale system behavior. Our research indicates that in an unconnected devices transmission model, a significant proportion of unconnected pairs results in a large number of connected devices with a specific scale parameter. We also discovered that scale and coherent scaling converge to the same outcome under certain conditions. Furthermore, our research discovered that a significant proportion of unconnected devices leads to predictable coherent scaling behavior in a single connected devices scenario, allowing for stable data transfer even when devices switch frequently. All findings are supported by computer simulations.

We introduce a novel approach to model the impact of non-gravitational forces in an N-body cosmological simulation framework, enabling the integration of various modified gravity theories and particle interactions beyond gravity. Our method involves developing a comprehensive set of N-body equations that incorporate the altered dynamics into a standard, widely-used numerical solver. By adopting this framework, we can perform rapid and exhaustive simulations of diverse modified gravity theories for any given particle interaction model, producing outputs comparable in quantity and quality to those from the Planck collaboration's simulations. As an example, we run simulations for the $\Lambda$CDM and conformally coupled dark matter f($R$) gravity models, demonstrating the feasibility and efficiency of our approach. Our code is accessible via GitHub under the license https://github.com/desmondshen/conformal-nbody.

Junper O'Connell's 2010 work on the Gaussian free field, initially defined on a rectangle and later connected to an asymptotic Karlin-McGregor measure, has been generalized. A new construction is proposed to achieve this connection through the combination of discrete Gaussian free fields and their limit, when defined on an expanding grid over a unit square. This construction enables a more expansive class of measure than previously attainable, offering insights into local regularity properties of the Gaussian free field. Specifically, it facilitates a better understanding of the local behavior at any point within the domain, when evaluated against the Gaussian free field measure. This approach could potentially be applied to investigate similar properties of two-dimensional gravity.

MediaWiki's Wikipedia has evolved into a diverse, dynamic, and collaborative knowledge-sharing platform. Its back-end is composed of numerous interconnected components, such as page histories, revision texts, and user discussion boards, offering a rich source of data. By mining this vast database, researchers can gain insights into the underlying mechanisms that drive the evolution of massively online collaborative projects (MOCPs). As new theories emerge to guide future developments, it is essential to clearly communicate these ideas to the community for feedback and collaboration. To address this need, we introduce WorkingWiki, an open-source platform built on top of MediaWiki API, enabling scholars to experiment with new theories in a controlled, transparent, and cooperative environment.

This study investigates the behavior of turbulent jet flames and their interaction with their surrounding environment, specifically focusing on how acoustic waves influence their dynamics. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers need detailed and efficient models that simulate the coupled fluid-flow, thermochemical reactions, and unsteady flame-wall interactions caused by sound. Current simulation techniques, while accurate, are computationally costly and lack a unified approach to reactions and boundary conditions, resulting in a lack of comprehensive models capable of capturing all these aspects simultaneously. To address this challenge, the work presents a detailed analysis of the response of turbulent methane jet flames to acoustic waves at approximately 450K, and develops efficient models using machine learning algorithms and active flame methods. The results show that the flame's response can be described by a set of mathematical equations, and the developed models, in combination, provide accurate and computationally feasible simulations of the flames and their surrounding environment.

In this paper, a novel method is presented for analyzing stellar oscillations using a geometric approach. A specific metric on the space of possible stellar configurations is employed to calculate the distance between the observed star and its closest counterpart in a reference manifold of equilibrium models. Notably, the distance calculated in this manner exhibits oscillatory behavior, revealing meaningful information about the star's internal composition. A case study, using Adiabatic stellar oscillations as an example, illustrates the advantages of this geometric approach in extracting physical insights from the oscillatory data.

A robust, globally applicable method is presented to discover two categories of dynamic strategies in neural networks: traveling chimera states and synchronized states. Using a distance metric that accounts for ordering and magnitude, this approach can identify distinct behavioral patterns in network models that exhibit a dynamic range of collective phenomena, excluding individualistic actions. Notably, we find that a FitzHugh-Nagumo model combined with slow adaptation exhibits traveling chimera states, which we analyze in terms of local stability, signal propagation, and robustness against external influences.

A computer simulation method is used to examine how clusters form and break apart in 2D lattice fluids when sites are connected, at both balanced and uneven temperatures. Our method differs from typical studies because it involves clusters composed of neighboring, isolated sites. We discover that equal temperatures across the system result in cluster sizes matching those created by sudden changes in lattice connectivity within the same temperature environment. Also, cluster breakdown at unequal temperatures follows the formation process within the same temperature conditions. Another interesting outcome arises when the system with equal temperatures has lower cluster entropy than its counterpart with sudden changes in lattice connectivity, despite the cluster entropy usually rising with cluster size.

In the study of neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) and the effective neutrino mass ($m_{\beta\beta}$), we investigate how ultralight dark matter (ULDM) could create time-varying changes in decay rates and look for any ultralight dark matter-induced signals. We find that, given current experimental data, existing limits on ULDM self-interaction and its interaction with the Higgs boson are not significantly impacted. However, more sensitive experiments could potentially reveal an annual modulation of neutrinoless double beta decay rates and thus reach more sensitive bounds on ULDM properties - an outcome that could be achieved with neutrinoless double beta decay experiments using BGO, $^{136}$Ce, CuInSe$_2$, and $^{130}$Ba-based sources. If future experiments observe neutrinoless double beta decay, we also discuss the potential to constrain ULDM properties from the observed spectrum of decay electrons, although this requires very high precision measurements that may be challenging to achieve. We also review the implications of ULDM on the expansion rate of the early universe and Big Bang nucleosynthesis, which could potentially inform neutrinoless double beta decay experiments about the properties of ULDM with masses between $10^{-14}$eV and $10^{-10}$eV. Finally, we summarize the implications of ULDM on cosmology and the large-scale structure of the universe.

The effects of solar magnetic field on ultra-high energy photons have been modeled, taking into account the magnetic field's ability to alter the flow of these photons as they approach Earth from space. A simple, yet effective method has been proposed for modifying the cosmic ray flux spectrum observed near Earth, by accounting for the interaction of these high-energy particles with the Sun's magnetic field. The proposed method was applied to the 2008 flux of ultra-high energy neutral cosmic rays above 10^14 GeV, and the resulting modifications to the flux were determined as a function of both observation time and energy level. Significant variations in the flux are expected to occur under certain conditions, specifically when observing the Sun rising above the horizon at certain times and when the solar flux levels approach that of the surrounding sky, particularly in energy levels exceeding 10^19 GeV.

Nonlocal gravity models based on root-inverted Einstein-Hilbert action are examined, with the case where the inversion coefficient equals negative one being particularly significant. In this scenario, the equations governing tetrads include an intrinsic nonlocal term that can be ignored for infinitesimally small metrics, thereby allowing for unique solutions. These solutions correspond to constitutive connections derived from constitutive metrics stemming from Einstein-Cartan fields. Furthermore, the framework is localized through the introduction of spin-2 fields into the Poincaré gauge group, with a resulting action resembling the Einstein-Cartan-Fock theory supplemented by a specific spin-2 field term.

Conflicting updates pose a significant challenge in creating replicated data structures that maintain consistency. A novel, crash-tolerant update strategy called E - W has been introduced to simplify the creation of such structures by ensuring the removal of redundant entries and the preservation of unique elements within each operation. This work delves into the elements of the E - W framework and provides several examples of conflict-free replicated data structures built using this approach, including atomic registers, stacks, queues, and sort lists. By incorporating performance and memory optimization techniques, researchers have demonstrated that some of these structures can achieve very low operation latencies, with results showing that optimized atomic queues and sort lists can be executed in as little as 344 nanoseconds and 306 nanoseconds, respectively, according to empirical measurements conducted on real hardware.

This study offers a detailed exploration of how functional genomic data and genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings can be used for complex human traits. We present several key points, including interpreting GWAS results through linkage disequilibrium, exploring alternative association statistical methods, and examining the genetic basis for multiple traits using multivariate methods. To illustrate these concepts, we undertake comprehensive analyses for 18 diverse human traits and summarize our findings. Multivariate and collaborative research designs have significantly boosted our comprehension of genotype-phenotype relationships, yet there is still room for improvement. For example, incorporating single-nucleotide functionality into sequencing data from whole-genome projects, as well as epigenomic information, can further refine our understanding. Integrating deep learning-based models for predicting association statistical methods is another area for potential advancement. Ultimately, advancing our knowledge of multiple human traits and diseases will require refining our statistical tools for genetic data and exploring more complex biological pathways, from molecular interactions to tissue-specific functionality.

This paper discusses the significance of studying rare events in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), specifically the conditions under which one proton interacts with another in the beam pipe rather than with its partner proton. These so-called "minor" systems, though uncommon, nonetheless occur with some frequency and have been demonstrated to be capable of producing high-transverse momentum particles even from initial-state radiation. Given that the LHC operates under high-intensity conditions, these "minor" systems can actually collide with multiple protons in a single beam, which has been found to create a unique environment for study. Based on theoretical calculations using e-p and i-p scattering cross-sections, the expected conditions at the LHC have been estimated, which, in turn, could allow for the investigation of hidden-sector physics through very specific types of decays of short-lived particles known as psions.

Historically, astronomers classified X-ray binary transients based on their recurrence patterns, defining long-period systems as those with recurrence intervals exceeding a factor of ten and short-period systems as those with intervals no more than a factor of three. A study was conducted to evaluate whether the time-averaged recurrence distributions of short- and long-period transients actually differ. The results revealed that approximately 40% of long-period transients have recurrence factors falling within the 3-10 range, which overlaps significantly with the distribution of short-period transients. Moreover, the density of short-period transients with recurrence factors greater than 100 is only twice that of transients with a factor of 10. It is proposed that the recurrence distributions of short- and long-period transients are not distinct but rather represent the same population viewed from different perspectives. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is that the X-ray luminosity of an accreting neutron star's state is governed by the rate of mass transfer across the innermost stable circular orbit. A theoretical model is proposed to explain the characteristics of the quiescent X-ray binaries in the vicinity of the Galactic Centre as an assembly of systems with overlapping circumbinary stability domains. According to this model, the quiescent binaries should exhibit recurrence periods spanning the entire spectrum from short to long.

The test known as the binary test validates general relativity by confirming the availability of weak gravitational waves that were recently detected for the first time. A prediction made by an alternative theory called DGP cosmology, this is no longer possible as it implies the emission of a large number of dark gravitons in order to account for the energy carried away. Consequently, the orbit of the binary system decays at a much faster rate. However, if there is an unusual interaction between dark energy and matter in such a way that prevents this energy loss from occurring, it becomes possible for the binary test to serve as a test for DGP cosmology. We conduct a thorough analysis of this interaction, formulating it within the framework of scalar-tensor theory. We then estimate the possible parameters of this interaction based on the observation of gravitational waves. As an outcome of this analysis, it is determined that the line on the test of binary gravitational waves appears as a frequency-dependent term in the phase evolution, and our analysis also allows us to predict that future detectors such as LISA will be able to measure this line with remarkable precision.

We investigated 8.4 GHz compact dim (C&D) radio sources in three nearby galaxies using data from the ATLO first local universe survey.  By analyzing total intensity and spectral index maps, approximately 500 new radio sources were identified in each galaxy after applying source extraction techniques.  When combining C&D sources within velocity channels or spectral bins, distinctive features emerged, revealing multiple characteristics.  As C&D sources became more compact, they exhibited higher spectral indices, lower flux density ratios between 8.4 GHz and 1.4 GHz, narrower velocity widths, and narrower frequency widths.  When visualized as an S-Sigma relationship, C&D sources with larger aperture sizes displayed higher surface brightnesses.  However, C&D sources of different sizes did not overlap when compared using the same scale, indicating that their physical properties are size-dependent.  These findings may offer valuable insights into the diverse mechanisms behind the production of radio sources across a wide range of scales.

This research analytically explores how shocks propagate through erupting stars due to random wave interactions and the spreading of sonic points. Key findings show that over time, in the one-dimensional model, the erosion of the erupting star's envelope accelerates at a rate of $t^{4/3}$, whereas in reality, it follows a different, more complex pattern. Our heuristic approach to this more complex scenario yields results that more accurately reflect wave-induced pressure and erosion of the envelope at specific times. These findings are relevant to various types of supernovae, including those resulting from massive star eruptions, and provide a basis for more complex, three-dimensional computer simulations.

We provide a comprehensive definition of a specific class of algebraic and linear objects, varying in dimensional pairs, that directly correspond to a subset of mathematical and non-mathematical weight spaces within the framework of classical Langlands program theory. For each pair of integer dimensional objects, we demonstrate associativity under composition, a fundamental property of a morphism operation. Our definition builds upon previously established definitions, incorporating additional structure of modular varieties and morphism operations, and is an extension of a previously proven result of associativity for a particular type of algebraic object denoted as phi-modular variational Hodge-Tate modules of pure type. Our work is based on a previously demonstrated connection between two specific types of objects denoted as local arithmetic comparison isomorphisms.

This study investigates the influence of molecular crystal dynamics on single-molecule switching devices, discovering that intrinsic motion-induced interactions can significantly impact electronic spacing and data stability. Unlike previously studied electron-phonon and spin-vibration couplings, these internal dynamics generate time-dependent changes, allowing data encoding via vibrational interactions rather than electronic ones. However, while linearized versions of these interactions yield similar results to their static counterparts, non-linearized versions reveal distinct, novel phenomena. Notably, strong irreversible energy transfer occurs between electrons and phonons under specific conditions, and data stability is compromised when molecular rotations reach resonance, creating unique devices for detecting electron-phonon coupling and rotational inertia.

$\tau$-tilting theory, a relatively new area within representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, has been frameworkized to represent various mathematical objects and facilitate potential applications. Its primary focus is on comprehending local, detailed aspects of an algebra's representation type. This introduction is designed to explain the fundamental concepts of $\tau$-tilting theory and frameworkized concepts associated with it. Additionally, the paper will highlight relationship between $\tau$-tilting theory and other representation-theoretic constructs, as well as discuss recent breakthrough results within this area.

Understanding how to interpret language relies on knowing the meaning of words, yet the precise definition of linguistic knowledge needed for communication remains unclear. This study utilizes data from human-human conversations to explore a wide range of meanings for familiar words within specific contexts. Our findings show that even for frequently used words, a single definition is insufficient; instead, there exists a diverse array of concepts associated with them. These concepts are not randomly selected but are interconnected, forming rich semantic networks. Furthermore, the relationships between these concepts facilitate the prediction of new meanings for the same word. This indicates that comprehending language may require mastering the entire concepts linked to words, instead of focusing on just a singular definition for each word.

Automated driving systems require advanced safety analysis using deep recognition of actions and hazard prediction from short video clips captured by front-facing cameras during the lane change process. This paper presents a new approach for identifying dangerous maneuvers and predicting potential risks by combining the transfer of segmentation masks with specialized deep neural networks that analyze temporal patterns in video data. Our method involves extracting segmentation masks from each video frame to create feature sequences, which are then processed to recognize complex behaviors and identify hazardous events like road entrapment and head-on collisions. Evaluations using real-world data show that our approach outperforms existing methods in accuracy for action recognition and hazard prediction.

The potential of young exoplanets and brown dwarfs to be heard from via their acoustic waves has been discussed in recent research. However, there is very little information on the subsurface of these celestial bodies that could distort any surface sound we might detect. Our study developed a computational model of solid-gas rotating planets and brown dwarfs, focusing on how the rotation affected the internal structure and gravitational field. Our research established the mass-shedding limit of solid-core gas巨行星, which occurs when a Jupiter-like planet with a 0.448 Earth radii solid core reaches a 0.34 times per orbit rotation rate without losing its matter. In contrast, massive brown dwarfs with 65-Jupiter masses would reach this limit with the same 0.34 times per orbit rotation rate, whereas smaller, lower-mass brown dwarfs or rapidly spinning Jupiter-like planets could theoretically emit audible surface sounds.

A new method has been developed to compare theoretical amplitude predictions with the observed data from the LHC, specifically in the process pp->WW^* ->lνll at CMS Com-13 TeV. The impact of various amplitude formulation approaches has been assessed, specifically the effect of unitarity-violating amplitude behavior at high energies has been studied. Two advanced amplitude frameworks were employed, namely the Primakoff and Coulomb amplitude formulations, and their respective performance was evaluated against the standard approach of adding amplitude components, referred to as the "naive" method. The modifications to amplitude components' effects were assessed using the CWEFT Lagrangian at three-loop accuracy, and found to significantly alter both amplitude predictions and the associated differential cross-sections. The study demonstrated that unitarity-breach effects substantially influence amplitude accuracy, and that adopting alternative amplitude formulation approaches can substantially modify amplitude behavior and, as a result, any deduction made about new physics from such calculations.

We've analyzed the post-launch behavior of various types of gamma-ray bursts, including typical, short, and odd cases, following a new hypothesis. This hypothesis proposes that the material surrounding collapsing massive stars or merging compact objects varies along a continuous spectrum. This variation is represented by a one-dimensional coordinate system, where each point represents a different type of gamma-ray burst, and the position determines the surrounding material's density. Based on the post-launch behavior of gamma-ray bursts, we've created a new diagram that shows their evolution. We've also observed that the afterglow light in gamma-ray bursts follows the same decay patterns and can be explained by the same physical processes, regardless of whether they're short, long, or odd cases. This suggests that the boundaries between these categories are blurry and that they all exist along the same one-dimensional coordinate system. Additionally, we've observed that the position of gamma-ray bursts in this coordinate system strongly influences their post-launch dynamics. Those with lazy movement tend to have bright early afterglows with radio waves dominating their light output. Those with active movement in active environments have vigorous gamma-ray movement and complex afterglow light outcomes. Finally, we've discussed how this new diagram can be applied to the classification of gamma-ray bursts and their host environments.

Bipartite vertex partitioning involves dividing a bipartite graph's vertex set into two equivalent sets, given that the graph has a sufficiently large number of edges in relation to its number of vertices. Our research offers a new approach to this problem by integrating two distinct methodological frameworks: one drawn from the fields of analytic combinatorics and combinatorial optimization, the other from restricted Turing machines and parameterized algorithms. As a result, our developed method significantly simplifies the previously most efficient complex solution, now also being a dynamic, parameterized, and Turing machine-based solution.

Our research aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of various image recognition models for settings characterized by initially adequate training data for one or more primary classes, with subsequent learning opportunities for novel classes. Models operating in such environments, which possess multiple Single-class and Novel classes, are referred to as 1NAILED scenarios. These settings, which incorporate the NAAILED framework, present challenging conditions due to their inclusion of several distinct classes of classes, each with its own degree of imbalance. A thorough examination was conducted on deep neural network approaches developed for these intricate settings, including a novel method called IN-C3IP. These algorithms were evaluated on two meticulously designed datasets, which were created by transferring existing classes to Novel classes from the PASCAL VOC 2007 collection. Despite achieving state-of-the-art results on standard incremental learning benchmarks, our findings reveal that models performing in NAAILED scenarios exhibit significantly higher levels of failure. A significant observation from our research is that ensemble methods and self-correction strategies exhibit the most promising results. However, they still suffer from considerable performance degradation.

This paper delves into the design of a bipedal robot's gait control system that utilizes propellants for assisted movement, addressing the limitations of electric-powered limbs in terms of size, weight, and torque. The proposed electric-hydraulic hybrid limb system leverages the advantages of both technologies to facilitate movement. A novel gait control method is put forth, enabling efficient and sturdy locomotion through a combination of phased motor-assisted propulsion, controlled propellant release, and precise timing. The results suggest that this approach can lead to improved movement efficiency and performance.

A residue field $T/M$ of a discrete valuation ring $V$ is considered "complete" if there's a ring homomorphism $\lambda: V \to T$ such that $\lambda(t) \equiv a \pmod M$ for some $a \in T$, with $M$ being the maximal ideal of $T$. In this note, we investigate the connection between the influential concept of a complete residue field and the completion of valued domains, with a focus on demonstrating that the valuation ring of the holomorphic function field within a Hilbert scheme is highly related to the celebrated result by Raynaud regarding the discrete valuation ring of the formal power series.

Modern high-performance processors, despite their impressive speed, suffer from significant security vulnerabilities. Recent breakthroughs in side-channel attacks, such as Spectre and Meltdown, expose the inefficiency of processor performance counters, which are optimized to measure and optimize processor throughput. These countermeasures, however, are insufficient in addressing such efficiency-based flaws. To further explore this uncharted territory, we introduce HyperDegrade, a novel side-channel attack that exploits the processors' efficiency optimization to introduce intentional performance degradations across a wider range of systems, from servers to laptops and even older computers. HyperDegrade goes beyond previous attacks by affecting two fundamental processor operations: instruction execution and memory access. Surprisingly, we discovered that even processors with built-in security vulnerabilities can be targeted with this efficient optimization-based side-channel attack. In our experiments, HyperDegrade was able to induce performance degradations of up to four GHz on modern processors, achieving a precise, fine-grained control of performance across three orders of magnitude, all while remaining undetected and leaving processors in a secure state. Furthermore, we developed advanced machine learning models based on these introduced degradations, which were able to accurately achieve near-impossible classification tasks with remarkable precision rates of up to ninety-nine percent, with significantly lower data requirements compared to similar attacks.

We investigate the possibility of the Higgs boson contributing to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment in order to fulfill its role in the electroweak naturalness hypothesis. Given the current constraints on the Higgs coupling to a yet-undiscovered scalar particle, we determine the maximum and minimum sizes of the contribution that the Higgs can make. Assuming a two-Higgs doublet model as a natural extension to the Standard Model, we find a maximum contribution of 0.24 x 10^-9, supported by specific parameters. However, within this same model, we consider two scenarios for the mass of the virtual scalar particle, located either below or above the 2m_t threshold. For the scenario below the threshold, we calculate a minimum contribution of 4.6 x 10^-9, supported by specific parameters. If the threshold is crossed, we find a minimum contribution of 5.9 x 10^-9, occurring when the virtual top quark and W boson contributions are opposed. These outcomes highlight a significant gap between the g-2 experimental and theoretical values, indicating that while the Higgs can contribute to the discrepancy, it cannot fully resolve the difference.

Using tree-level data from the Spallanzanti experiment, two different approaches were used to determine the value of gamma. The first approach used the maximum likelihood method, while the first and second moments were employed in the second. The results for gamma were found to be 0.56 ± 0.16 through the maximum likelihood method, and 0.51 ± 0.16 through the moment-based method. The outcomes for gamma from both methods matched each other within the margin of error. The results were also compared to previous findings from the Spallanzanti experiment and the Super-Kamiokande experiment, and the value of gamma was constrained to be less than or equal to 0.70 at a 90% confidence level.

A knot or link is equivalent when one can be deformed into the other without cutting the rope, and this equivalence can be established through a set of moves, including the 3-move, 4-move, and the welded move, which allows for self-intersections at the same point in space. The E-equivalence, which considers the welded move, is distinct from the classical knot theory's three-ball homeomorphism for most complicated knots or links, and it is easier to demonstrate for some, like the Whitehead link, and certain torus knots, and it is established that the 3-move alone is never enough to achieve E-equivalence for any knot or link, combining it with the welded move to reach E-equivalence for a broad set of knots or links, and a new class of 3-move reversible welded-unknotting moves for this set, and an induction-based approach using a particular unknotting procedure for these 3-move reversible welded-moves.

We prove that the semifield of rational functions on a tropical curve $\Gamma$ is finitely generated over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}[\mathbb{Q}]$ by finding a finite set of functions that, when combined with polynomial additions, cover the entire semifield. This result is further restricted to subsemifields of the tropical functions on $\Gamma$, and we explore its implications for questions of integral dependence within the semifield.

We demonstrate that the long-studied Fox-Hatcher loop, initially identified by Fox in 1957 and later re-discovered by Vassiliev in 1990, is a Vassiliev loop of the lowest order - a Vassiliev loop with an associated invariant that has a derivative of +1 at its first differentiation. Following 1990, many Vassiliev loop invariants have been discovered, but none are linear like the Fox-Hatcher loop. We find that the Fox-Hatcher loop generates a order three invariant in the algebra of Casson-Walker invariant. Additionally, we prove that the Cyclic Vassiliev conjugating element in the fundamental group of the complement of a link has characteristic of order three as a module, and this characteristic is found to be the smallest possible.

New research from the KATRIN experiment has yielded accurate measurements of neutrino mass-related data derived from triangular inequalities, resulting in minimum possible values for the electron neutrino mass spectrum ($m_1,m_2,m_3$). To obtain minimum possible values for $m_1,m_2$, researchers applied assumptions that two of the mass values are identical and occurred at the present time, while applying similar constraints to $m_3$ required assuming $m_1=m_2$. Based on these conditions, the research established upper limits on the square root of the product of the three mass values ($\sqrt{m_1m_2m_3}$), establishing a minimum possible value of $0.048$ eV, and under specific conditions, established minimum possible values for $m_1,m_2,m_3$. Furthermore, comparing these findings with research on cosmic observations regarding cosmic neutrino background and laboratory research on the Casimir effect, the research established that the minimum possible values for the masses of the three types of neutrinos must be at least $0.048$ eV, and that under specific conditions, the minimum possible values for the masses of the three types of neutrinos are $0.016$ eV ($m_1$), $0.041$ eV ($m_2$), and $0.010$ eV ($m_3$).

A evolução dos computadores tem sido impulsionada pela necessidade constante de maior velocidade de processamento. Com a frequência de processadores atingindo limites físicos, a abordagem de paralelização tem-se mostrado eficaz para contornar este gargalo. Este trabalho compara duas métodos de cálculo de multiplicação de matrizes, a abordagem sequencial (processador) e a abordagem paralela (processador gráfico), com o objetivo de demonstrar a eficácia da unidade gráfica no processamento de grandes matrizes.

The successful execution of group tasks for robots demands effective collaboration through real-time communication and processing of the environment. To achieve this, we've developed a decentralized system that enables robots to cooperate by leveraging network-based communication to anticipate and process information, a feature we've tested with a standard set of robots performing welds on a triangular pattern. Our approach shows that even with limited computation and communication, robots can collaborate to complete complex tasks when provided with appropriate predictive processing, one feature we've tested with a trio of robots successfully doing a weld on a triangular pattern.

To incorporate rigorous high-energy corrections into amplitude-based predictions for QCD-driven processes, a method known as 'renormalization of amplitudes' has been developed. Initially, these calculations were limited to leading transverse effects due to the influence of alpha_s^2 squared terms. This study explores the possibility of applying the renormalization of transverse anomalies to processes within quenching PDEQCD, particularly within the context of forward parton distributions. Our investigation suggests that this application may demand the inclusion of discontinuous terms with derivatives, potentially challenging the conventional factorization framework.

This document introduces the problem of pragmatic privacy breaches in vertical federated learning models. In VFL frameworks, multiple organizations collaborate to train a predictive model without revealing sensitive data. However, research has revealed that individual organizations can exploit their own unique data row information to predict the secret information held by other participants. Two prominent VFL protocols, Secure Multi-Party Learning based on Multiparameter Hashing (SMPC-MPH) and Secure Vertical Learning (SVFL), have been found vulnerable to this type of privacy assault. We examine the conditions under which these attacks can occur and develop more efficient methods of execution. We also assess the level of vulnerability associated with different VFL protocols and the ability of an attacker to successfully launch attacks. Finally, we provide guidance on mitigating the risks posed by these attacks.

Nonparametric density estimation is a statistical method whose accuracy is compromised by an unknown smoothness parameter, necessitating a compromise that affects its performance. k-NN estimation adapts to the parameter but suffers from inefficiency due to its nonoptimal rate of convergence. We develop a series of kernel estimators based on a set of independently and identically distributed transformations, which fall within the Skew-Mixed Fourier Transform framework. Our 'trial' estimators gain independence from the bandwidth parameter, enabling selection of an optimal estimator through data-driven choices such as cross-validation or historical methods. We prove that at smoothness points, specific estimators achieve the same smoothness-dependent optimal convergence rate as Daubechies-Meyer estimators, which k-NN fails to reach. Our kernel estimators utilize an exponentially decreasing kernel, which provides superior performance compared to the parabolic kernel in simulation studies.

This paper delves into the representation of groups that operate on products of sets by various permutations, focusing on Cartesian partitions and the corresponding group behavior. We provide a method for constructing irreducible representations using the Cartesian partition approach, and then apply it to analyze the direct product of groups, obtaining a new method for deriving irreducible representations of direct products, and also examining the wreath products of two groups.

This research investigates the Mobius scalar curvature, a new quantity defined on conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space with a non-zero mean curvature. 
We establish an upper bound for the Mobius scalar curvature on closed hypersurfaces in n-dimensional space, specifically where the WROH condition is met by a sufficient amount. 
Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the Mobius scalar curvature and the mean curvature, which is expressed as a product of the Mobius scalar curvature and the sum of a function of the mean curvature and a function of the WROH invariant. 
These findings are then applied to a class of hypersurfaces with a constant WROH invariant and a constant mean curvature, yielding a lower bound for their first principal curvature.

Advances in robotics and imaging technology have accelerated pediatric cardiac surgery, yet developing computer-aided tools for young patients is challenging due to limited datasets and varied anatomy in children. Previous studies have created automated segmentation models for several cardiac structures using U-Net, but these programs struggle to accurately identify deformed anatomy in patients with complex congenital heart conditions. This limits their effectiveness in providing computer-aided tools for surgical planning for these patients. This study assesses how well existing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based software packages perform in patients with severe congenital heart defects, specifically using two commonly used programs in adult patients and evaluating their performance in two rare conditions: hypoplastic left heart syndrome and single ventricle anatomy. By using clinical data from patients undergoing open-heart surgery, this study evaluates program accuracy and identifies the main difficulties these software packages face with pediatric patients' anatomy. This study's findings highlight the need for the development of new, condition-specific automated segmentation tools to improve surgical planning for patients with complex congenital heart defects.

This paper examines the asymptotic behavior of certain evolution models that depend on a small parameter $\varepsilon$, characterizing the material's microstructure. Our analysis involves obtaining convergence rates in a given rate function $W$, involving the gradient of the solution $u^\varepsilon$, as the material's heterogeneity becomes more fine-grained. Our findings are illustrated with specific material models and a general framework, as well as a concrete application to the Navier-Stokes-Darcy system.

A wireless network utilizing SWIPT, where transmission-receiving devices obtain power and data simultaneously, faces an issue of incompatible objectives. To overcome this challenge, we propose a flexible wireless system that uses power-signal separation to enable SWIPT to transmit two types of data at once. We develop an optimization model to determine the most effective allocation of time and power between power-bearing and data transmissions. We investigate a range of scenarios based on varying levels of time allocated to power transmissions. In order to achieve optimal allocation of time and polarizations across these scenarios, we formulate and solve the corresponding optimization problems, leveraging convex optimization techniques when necessary. A novel application in a hospital environment is explored to demonstrate the versatility of our proposed system in a real-world setting.

Multivariate sampling strategies, such as those used in learning pools and recommendations, can be enhanced significantly when side information is readily available. When tasked with a large number of potential options, these strategies often aim to achieve high efficiency by minimizing the number of options that need to be evaluated, relying on a subset known as the sampling rate. Traditionally, this group of methods assumes unlimited options but requires frequent evaluation of each one. In a recent experiment, our research team focused on low-density scenarios, such as those with high-frequency items and a diverse range of potential choices that need to be fully assessed. In response to these findings, our research designed the Fully Efficient Fully Contextualized (FEFC) framework, which integrates advanced techniques like reweighting and contextualization to efficiently address these challenges. Our results demonstrate the success of this framework in achieving accurate and consistent performance across a range of tests, such as the Amazon products dataset, the YouTube domain dataset, and a custom-built one.

In recent research on stochastic processes like M/G/1 and random walks, scholars have focused on analyzing the asymptotic behavior of conditional processes given they stay within specific boundaries. These studies often reveal interesting results about the processes' behavior under a certain condition, particularly their behavior under extreme conditions which can have valuable applications in finance and insurance. However, existing theoretical frameworks fall short of addressing these questions effectively. To overcome these limitations, new research has developed new theoretical models that provide detailed insights into the behavior of random walks and queueing systems under extreme conditions, providing new theoretical frameworks and simplified proofs for these models.

A word's clarity is crucial for accurate comprehension of text, but the ambiguity of word meanings remains a significant challenge in processing language. Unlike prior work that focuses solely on accurate understanding, our goal is to clarify word meanings through the creation of word representations that incorporate semantic information. Building upon the OnsBert model, which combines text and explaining words, our contribution is a word meaning clarification system based on the GlossBERT model. We extend the language capabilities of GlossBERT by incorporating a relevance ranking stage, allowing it to construct sentences describing the meaning of target words. Our experiments on the noun phrase benchmark demonstrate that our method outperforms the original language model of GlossBERT in terms of similarity, as well as several baseline models. Our work provides a feasible solution for enhancing semantic information in processing language models.

Effectively sequencing multimodal instructions is crucial for creating high-quality guides for complex tasks that require combining multiple modalities.
However, there is no clear consensus on the key aspects of instructional sequencing when dealing with more than a basic number of steps across various modalities.
To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted an in-depth study of multimodal procedural expertise by having 46 participants complete four complicated tasks based on instructional guides made up of modally mixed instructions involving assembling a bicycle, making a pizza, building a Lego house, and balancing a chemical equation.
Our findings revealed important insights into how people comprehend and follow instructions when multiple modalities are involved, highlighting specific sequencing patterns for tasks of increasing complexity.
Additionally, our study produced actionable recommendations for designing sequential multimodal instructions across different task scenarios.
These insights are supported by existing theories on procedural comprehension and have practical implications for the development of advanced instructional guide systems that can adapt to specific contexts and user needs.

Prior research on network breakdown has been confined to the analysis of large clusters using binary generating functions, which limited it to studying the parameters near the critical threshold. In contrast, this study develops an algorithm capable of creating triads - or triplets - of nodes within an extensive cluster following a Cayley tree structure, accurately reflecting the full distribution without critical parameter constraints. The study utilizes the triad algorithm to investigate the complete distribution of an extensive avalanche within the small-world network formed by the small-world prefabricated scale-free network (SSPN), and finds results that contrast with previous hypotheses on the distribution of network components formed when broken bonds occur randomly, which proved insufficient to explain the actual distribution of the (SSPN) cluster. The triad algorithm is also capable of producing the entire distribution of clusters that maintain their circular integrity within an hour after simulated bond destruction, which does not closely resemble the cluster distribution of an extensive avalanche in an SSPN network.

In this study, we introduce and analyze the universal Airy polynomials, which can be correlated with the asymptotic behaviors of several polynomial families, such as Hermite-polynomials of growing degree, as well as the Airy-polynomials of escalating coefficient parameter. Additionally, we derive a Stieltjes transform equation for the universal Airy measure and obtain explicit formulas for its moments.

For optical gravitational wave detectors, a high sensitivity at frequent wave frequencies is critical. Typically, researchers employ multiple mirrors to increase the effective length of detection areas. However, this strategy has its downsides, as it also amplifies the impact of optical fluctuations. In this investigation, we propose a novel approach called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, which utilizes the movement of all mirrors as a collective to become sensitive to optical fluctuations while minimizing the impact of internal reflections. In simulated scenarios representing the frequency range of 100Hz to 1kHz, this method has been shown to provide equivalent or better sensitivity than the standard technique of extending the detection area.

Researchers are actively exploring massive MIMO systems with L-shaped arrays for their potential to simplify radio electronics while improving initial access efficiency and downlink performance. However, our analysis using a stochastic geometry model reveals that visibility regions in an XL-MIMO system with an L-shaped array can have disconnected parts, which poses challenges for existing random access protocols that rely on initial access. Our simulation results show that as the number of antennas increases, the probability of forming intersecting visibility regions increases significantly, regardless of user distribution. Our findings suggest that such regions enable efficient intersection-based random access, which could benefit future XL-MIMO system design.

Our previous research revealed that gravitational instabilities in accretion disks can spawn spiral arms composed of clumps and filaments at their intersections. This study focused on predicting the characteristics of these structural features in the millimeter-wavelength continuum based on the mid-infrared temperature distributions examined in Paper I. A simplified model was employed to calculate the continuum emission from an atomic vertical shear-instability clump, filaments, and tortuous filaments, utilizing three-dimensional radiative equilibrium simulations. Results indicated that clumps would appear as bright submillimeter sources with a millimeter spectrum rising towards shorter wavelengths, whereas they would seem dimmer at millimeter wavelengths due to lower electron scattering opacity. VSI-stabilized disk portions would result in brighter millimeter and submillimeter spectra for features like tortuous filaments due to their thicker pressure-supported boundaries. Distinguishing between clumps under VSI equilibrium and collapse might be feasible by comparing their millimeter and submillimeter appearances, although further studies on clump growth and interactions with the protoplanet formation process are necessary.

A new calculation of the binding energy for the ${}^{40}\mathrm{Ca}$ atom reveals an unusually high stability, indicating electron contributions that are five times greater than previously estimated. This finding suggests a need to reevaluate theoretical models of electron interactions already supported by experimental evidence, such as accurate measurements of the ${}^{40}\mathrm{Ca}$ atomic energy. It is speculated that electron contributions to the binding energy of neutral calcium atoms may be disproportionately high compared to nuclear forces. Based on a rough estimation, this high electron-to-nuclear force ratio is believed to be stable across neutral calcium atoms, charged calcium ions, certain calcium-containing nuclei like those found in ${}^{40}\mathrm{Ca}$ atoms and atoms of other elements, as well as neutron stars. It is hypothesized that applying an 11 times greater electron-to-nuclear force ratio found in ${}^{40}\mathrm{Ca}$ atoms to proton-electron systems in neutron stars could explain their stability. It is also suggested that calculations of electron forces based on this high ratio in ${}^{40}\mathrm{Ca}$ atoms, when combined with nuclear forces, may better explain matter stability, including the stability of neutral atoms made up of protons, neutrons, and electrons.

Using spin-only exchange interactions as an approximation, previous studies have effectively explained the electronic and orbital characteristics of many perovskite manganites. However, this simplification overlooks the impact of correlated d-electrons on those very orbitals. Through comprehensive self-consistent calculations of the DMFT+SDPA model for SrMnO$_3$, we found that treating the actual frequency axis is crucial for accurately describing the system. The position and number of occupied and non-occupied bands are significantly influenced by p-d hybridizations, a finding corroborated by experimental data. The DMFT+SDPA approach naturally divides the d-bands into three groups - lower, middle, and upper - based on their filling status. The positions of these bands relative to the O 2p bands are entirely dependent on the p-d hybridization strength. The success of the spin-only exchange approximation in describing the middle band dynamics is limited, in contrast to its widespread use.

We propose an upgraded version of the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate that operates reliably, regardless of variations in the pulse sequence's amplitude. The enhanced gate utilizes a new amplitude-insensitive method, driven by the collective motion of a ion chain and its first mode's fundamental vibrations. The gate's performance is optimized through the use of three vibrations where the amplitude has a negligible effect on its operation and the contribution of two adjacent modes, adjacent mode-contribution, is also significant. The theoretical duration of the gate is calculated at approximately 2 microseconds and can be minimized to around 1.2 microseconds using a specific two-mode approach. The amplitude-sensitive and equal-contribution schemes can be applied to various configurations of ion traps by adding a linear drive to specific modes of vibration. The new gate is suitable for the construction of universal quantum computers and can be applied to optimization problems using the quantum annealing architecture with a minimal overhead of around 0.4 microseconds and can be used to produce highly entangled states like the cat state, GHZ state, and BELL pairs within 2.5 microseconds and around 3.6 microseconds, respectively, in a two-ion system. The new gate can also create a precision metrology state with a quantum Fisher information value of approximately 2.5 microseconds and can be optimized for maximum precision with a two-mode approach that contributes equally to adjacent modes, resulting in a quantum Fisher information value of around 1.2 microseconds and a

Recent high-resolution imaging techniques have enabled precise analysis of the atomic structure in ferroelectric materials, yet their ability to resolve the structure of paraelectric samples has been limited to general observations of disorder. Using hydrogen paraelectric perovskites as a test case, this study presents a detailed, precision analysis of structural disorder in materials such as $\mathrm{BaH_2}$ and $\mathrm{PbH_2}$, employing the PAW-3 method to resolve 18 independent atomic positions in the $Pnma$ phase. The results indicate that certain atoms maintain well-defined local symmetries, aligned with specific atoms in adjacent unit cells, forming distinct clusters of interacting paraelectric domains. Molecular dynamics simulations based on these structural findings support the existence of different domain types observed experimentally and illustrate the transition between domain states, illustrating the ability of local interactions to govern the behavior of paraelectric materials. The combination of advanced imaging and modeling techniques provides a foundation for understanding the dynamics of hydrogen migration and the design of more effective hydrogen storage systems.

Using a Dirac Hamiltonian, we examine the strongly correlated properties of a four-fermion, on-site repulsion system derived from generic, gapped Dirac bands. Our findings suggest that strong repulsion can transform a Dirac metal into an insulator with significant four-particle correlation, characterized by a distinct energy scale and a non-vanishing polarization. Next, we develop a correlated Dirac-Berry curvature framework to estimate the energy scale and correlation charge through geometric and topological parameters. Finally, we verify these estimates using exact diagonalization and quantum Monte Carlo methods.

A frequently encountered phenomenon in nature and human behavior is synchronous activity occurring at vastly different frequency scales, for example, a human's walking gait, which encompasses swing frequencies around 1 Hz and joint frequency expansion at approximately 10 Hz. Current methods for analyzing such data often treat the unimodal distributions of each frequency component independently. Nonetheless, they are intrinsically linked through a physical or functional mechanism, for example, the length of a leg determining the frequency at which it swings. To capture these complex relationships, we propose a new approach for modeling bimodal data consisting of under- and over-sampled frequency components and their unimodal distributions of each component, for instance, through a Gaussian curve for each frequency, while also exploring the relationship between them, for instance, using a copula. The resulting bimodal frequency and ratio (BIMFAR) model provides a comprehensive analytical tool for multimodal temporal signals, enabling the dissection of high-frequency signals into their constituent unimodal distributions of each component. Furthermore, BIMFAR can facilitate feature extraction for machine learning applications, for instance, in gait analysis.

This study explores the potential to study the neutral lepton N in the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ reaction with the NA62 experiment at a rate of 10^11 per day, focusing on scenarios where N is a massive particle that could be observed. By analyzing kinematic and other relevant factors, we estimate the detection sensitivity of the experiment to N and identify optimal research areas to test detection capabilities.

In a setup involving a Sagnac interferometer, we investigated how spectral changes occur due to the rotation's effect on the effective path length of the apparatus, which is influenced by its interaction with the hypothetical gravitational field and the gravitational redshift, all in a non-inertial rotating frame. By analyzing this interaction in a non-inertial frame, we calculated the spectral shift and determined that it aligns with the changes observed in a rotating Sagnac interferometer. Furthermore, we derived that the spectral shift is directly proportional to the angular velocity and the area enclosed within the interferometer. By extending this analysis to a stationary, non-rotating apparatus, we found that the spectral shift vanishes. By comparing our theoretical predictions to existing experimental data, we determined that current technology is capable of verifying our theoretical framework.

We introduce the concept of parabolic adjoint, establish connections with Weierstrass segments and components within the nilfibre, and demonstrate how to compute the Weierstrass segment component function using parabolic adjoint in specific cases. These developments extend earlier research by Hivert, The and Reutenauer into the domain of free associative algebras. Moreover, we define the sequences of Weierstrass segment and parabolic adjoint sequences, which are shown to be Weierstrass sequences for suitable starting elements in the free associative algebra in multiple variables. Having shwon the Weierstrass sequence and parabolic adjoint sequence coincide for nilpotent elements, we outline criteria for these sequences in general and provide explicit formulas for the parabolic adjoint sequences in certain cases.

Recently, there has been substantial success with neural language models, utilizing the Transformer architecture. However, it's intriguing to revisit classic models like $N$-gram models this year due to their remarkable performance and efficiency on hardware systems like microcontrollers. By combining the best of both worlds, we propose a residual learning approach where the $N$-gram model serves as an initial model for creating content, and a neural model is trained to match its distribution. Our experiments reveal that our neural creator models not only match the efficiency of the $N$-gram model but also surpass it in creation speed and output quality on multiple datasets using bi-gram, $n$-gram models (4-6 grams), and KRW models (around 100MB). Furthermore, we plan to utilize high-entropy $N$-gram probabilities to reduce calculation during sampling in our model.

We establish a connection between the study of $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties and the research into $\tau$-log-terminal singularities by demonstrating that the endomorphism of the Laurent operator $\mathcal{L}$ at a specific point can represent a $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety in a given ambient space $\mathbb{P}^{N+M}$. This connection can further illustrate the singular nature of the mapping through the behavior of the endomorphism of $\mathcal{L}$. This theory is supported by the construction of distinct $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties through various Laurent operators, as well as the decomposition of closed subvarieties based on their interaction with the image of $\mathcal{L}$.

This research presents an innovative method for generating 3D face models under various lighting and pose conditions, which are common challenges in real-world scenarios. Unlike conventional approaches that create a single 3D face model from an input image, our network predicts two face models from one input image and employs a self-alignment loss to determine the optimal matching pair. We call this innovative approach the Self-Aligned Dual Face Reconstruction network. By allowing our system to learn from two potentially inaccurate predictions rather than a precise one, we enhance its performance under varying conditions. Our results show significant improvements in our system's accuracy and robustness when dealing with the AFW and IJB-A datasets. Additionally, our framework can be applied to other single-image 3 face regression methods to yield even better performance.

The authors discuss current developments in model Hamiltonians that incorporate higher-order derivatives and gauge fields of those types, used for studying exotic phenomena like mode softening, spatially localized charges, and broken translational symmetries. They propose a new, user-friendly framework for constructing these models by utilizing an efficient parameterization of the vector potential. As a case study, they examine a model exhibiting spontaneously disrupted translational symmetry, involving the Graviton and a "fracton" derived from the Galileon, and demonstrate the ability to manipulate the mass of the fracton by adjusting the gauge field parameters, ultimately achieving confinement.

This paper examines an inflationary model based on a specific $\alpha$-attractor type kinetic term, where the potential is transformed into an anharmonic form.
